recipe.history:
Sage — Salvia officinalis — takes its genus name from the Latin word salvare, meaning to save or to heal, a testament to the herb's millennia-long reputation as a medicinal plant of exceptional power. Native to the northern shores of the Mediterranean, particularly the coastal regions of what are now Croatia, Albania, and the Dalmatian coast, sage was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as a herb of preservation and purification. The Romans used it in religious ceremonies, the Greeks administered it as a tonic for memory and longevity — a tradition that persists in the folk medicine of many cultures to this day, with modern research suggesting some basis for sage's claimed cognitive benefits. During the Middle Ages, sage was among the most valued plants in the monastic herb garden, grown by Benedictine monks and recommended in herbalist texts as a treatment for everything from fever to snake bite. The English proverb 'He who has sage in his garden needs no physician' captures the extravagance of the claims made on its behalf. In cooking, sage has been central to Italian cuisine for centuries — saltimbocca alla romana layers sage with veal and prosciutto; sage butter (burro e salvia) is the classic dressing for pasta, particularly in the north of Italy; and in Tuscany, sage is tucked under the skin of roasted birds and stuffed into porchetta along with rosemary and garlic. In Britain, sage and onion stuffing became the defining Christmastime preparation, inseparable from roast goose and turkey.

Sage's presence in American cooking arrived through British colonial traditions, where sage and onion stuffing was transplanted directly from the English kitchen to the New England one, becoming Thanksgiving's aromatic backbone. In the American South, sage seasoned pork sausage — the crumbled breakfast sausage still sold in tubes bears sage as its defining note. Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, dried sage was a fixture in the American spice rack, used in stuffings, sausages, and roasts. The craft cooking renaissance of the late 20th century reintroduced fresh sage as a primary ingredient rather than a background seasoning. Fried sage leaves — a preparation common in northern Italian cooking — became fashionable as a garnish: the leaves fried in butter or oil until crisp, their volatile oils transforming from sharp and camphor-like when raw to something mellower, nuttier, and deeply savory when cooked. Sage brown butter, in which the milk solids in butter are cooked to nuttiness while sage leaves infuse the fat, became a canonical restaurant preparation. On a burger, fried sage provides textural crunch and herbal intensity; sage brown butter acts as a baste and sauce, transforming the entire composition.

Sage entered my cooking life through an accident that proved formative. I had bought a large bunch of fresh sage at a farmers market — more than I could possibly use before it turned — and decided to fry some of it simply to use it up. I heated a small pool of butter in a skillet, dropped in a handful of leaves, and watched them sizzle and curl and darken to a deep translucent green. I blotted them on paper towels, ate one, and was struck by the transformation: the raw sharpness was gone, replaced by something almost nutty, with a toasted quality and an herbal intensity that was warm rather than sharp. The butter left in the pan, darkened to a deep hazelnut color and fragrant with sage, I poured over a bowl of pasta with Parmesan, and it was one of the best things I had made all year. A few months later I made a burger basted in sage brown butter and topped with fried sage leaves and understood that I had been approaching this combination from the wrong direction all along: the burger was always the right destination.

Sage brown butter basting is most effective on a patty cooked to medium rare — 130–135°F — because at that temperature the patty's exterior crust is fully developed and able to absorb the basted butter without becoming soggy, while the interior remains pink and juicy enough to contrast with the richness of the butter. Basting happens in the final minutes of cooking: the butter is added to the pan, the sage leaves are added to infuse it, the pan is tilted, and the foaming brown butter is spooned repeatedly over the surface of the patty. This both bastes the crust with fat and aromatizes the entire surface with sage. A well-done patty can tolerate basting but has nothing left to give — the moisture is already gone. A medium rare patty receives the basting butter as a gift, its surface soaking up the nutty, herbal richness while the interior stays exactly as it should be: soft, pink, and absolutely alive.
ingredients: 2 tbsp olive oil (for dimpling and baking)
12 fresh sage leaves (pressed into dough tops before baking)
24 large fresh sage leaves, stems removed
1 cup neutral oil (canola or vegetable) for frying
For the sage brown butter sauce:
For the butternut squash and apple relish:
1 cup butternut squash, peeled and finely diced (¼-inch cubes)
1 small Granny Smith apple, peeled, cored, and finely diced
½ cup crème fraîche or sour cream
2 tbsp fresh sage, very finely minced
Salt and white pepper to taste
4 slices aged Fontina or Taleggio cheese
instructions: 1. Make the focaccia buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture and ¼ cup olive oil. Knead on medium 8 minutes until smooth. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1–1½ hours until doubled.

2. Preheat oven to 425°F. Oil a rimmed baking sheet generously. Press dough into an even rectangle approximately 12x9 inches. Drizzle with remaining 2 tbsp olive oil and dimple vigorously with your fingertips. Press 2 fresh sage leaves into the top of each section you'll cut into buns. Sprinkle generously with flaky sea salt. Let rest uncovered 20 minutes. Bake 18–22 minutes until deep golden. Cool, then cut into 6 square or rectangular buns. Slice horizontally.

3. Make the butternut squash and apple relish: Melt butter in a small skillet over medium heat. Add diced squash and cook 5–6 minutes until beginning to soften and brown in spots. Add diced apple, brown sugar, apple cider vinegar, cinnamon, and cayenne. Cook, stirring, 4–5 more minutes until squash is tender, apple is softened, and the mixture is slightly jammy. Season with salt. Remove from heat.

4. Make the sage cream sauce: Combine crème fraîche, minced sage, lemon juice, and grated garlic. Season with salt and white pepper. Stir thoroughly and refrigerate at least 30 minutes to let the sage infuse.

5. Fry the sage leaves: Heat about ½ inch of neutral oil in a small saucepan to 350°F. Working in small batches, carefully drop sage leaves into the hot oil. They will sizzle vigorously and are done in 20–30 seconds when they have darkened slightly and the sizzling quiets. Remove with a slotted spoon onto paper towels. Immediately season with flaky salt. They crisp up further as they cool.

6. Make the sage brown butter sauce: Melt butter in a small light-colored saucepan over medium heat. When the foam subsides and the milk solids begin to turn golden, add the sage leaves and sliced garlic. The butter will foam again. Cook, swirling, 1–2 minutes until the butter is deep nutty brown and the sage is fragrant. Add lemon juice carefully (it will spatter). Season with salt. Keep warm.
7. Form patties: Gently combine ground beef with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and dried sage. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

8. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side. Flip. Add butter and fresh sage leaves to the pan. Tilt the pan and baste continuously with the foaming sage butter for 1–2 minutes. Add Fontina or Taleggio to each patty and cover briefly to melt. Remove when internal temperature reads 130–135°F for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast buns: Use the same pan over medium heat with residual butter to toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread sage cream sauce on both cut sides of each bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted cheese on the bottom bun. Add a spoonful of butternut squash and apple relish alongside. Top with a handful of baby spinach. Pile 5–6 fried sage leaves on top. Drizzle a small spoonful of sage brown butter over everything, letting it pool slightly. Finish with flaky sea salt. Cap and serve immediately.
